sm: Hosts Mary Reichard and Nick Eicher open the Monday, November 16th episode, and Kent Covington reads the news. Air travel is returning to normal after Friday's nationwide ground stop, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy traced to a contractor replacing copper lines with fiber optic cable, with no sign of a cyber attack. In Israel, Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot are discussing a unity government but disagree on who would lead it. Israel killed a top Hamas commander, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed a strike on a radar system at a US base in Bahrain, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian death threats forced his family onto a military base. President Trump heads to Asia for talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on nuclear weapons. SpaceX also caught a Starship spacecraft at its launch tower for the first time.

The Legal Docket segment starts with a Supreme Court case from Fulton County, Georgia. Jasmine Young sued the district attorney's office for pregnancy discrimination, and the office raised a defense, that she was personal staff of the elected DA, only late, in a summary judgment motion. The justices debated whether the delay's lack of harm to Young is enough or whether the office needed to show good cause. The main story is a North Dakota dispute. Rancher Leonard Hoffman and others fought WBI Energy Transmission, a private pipeline company using federal eminent domain. A district judge ordered WBI to pay just under 400,000 dollars in legal fees under state law, but the appeals court reversed, saying the federal standard applies. Ranchers' lawyer Robert McNamara argued the Fifth Amendment sets a floor, not a ceiling. Justice Kagan noted this would make pipelines much harder to build.

Justice Kavanaugh said adding attorney's fees piece by piece raises costs for consumers. Pipeline lawyer Paul Hughes argued that federal power brings the federal compensation standard with it, and the Justice Department backed the company. The ranchers answered that a private company is not the federal government, and a friend of the court brief cited historical cases of private firms paying more, including attorney fees. Hoffman said the case is about protecting the legacy of the land. Then Nick Eicher talks with financial analyst David Bahnsen about NVIDIA, where Jensen Huang has suddenly left amid a scandal. Bahnsen says he cannot see the company coming out stronger, though it must now build a real succession plan. He calls NVIDIA more like the hedge fund than the central bank of the AI moment, and says Huang's relationships are hard to replace.

Bahnsen says skepticism about NVIDIA's financing arrangements would have come up with or without Huang. He points to the coming Anthropic IPO as a key domino, since many commitments depend on it, and says NVIDIA is entangled as lender, owner and counterparty. He adds that NVIDIA has booked more chips than can be used, and that this does not mean a house of cards, but there is hidden risk. On Washington, he notes Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly criticized Commerce over restrictions meant to stop AI chips reaching China, and Commerce Secretary Lutnik was told to preserve documents. Bahnsen says the two men dislike each other and one will likely have to go, probably Lutnik, though Trump has been loyal. He says lax enforcement would hurt the national security case for tariffs.

The World History Book looks at Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, reported by Kristen Flavin. In 2013 Holmes introduced a small blood collection device, and she later founded her pitch on faster, cheaper tests from a finger prick on a machine called the Edison. Theranos had a board with Henry Kissinger, James Mattis and George Shultz, a Walgreens deal for 40 Arizona pharmacies, over 700 million dollars raised, and a valuation near 9 billion. Employee Tyler Shultz, George Shultz's grandson, and others found the machines gave wildly inaccurate results, and Holmes secretly used modified commercial machines for demonstrations. John Carreyrou's 2015 Wall Street Journal exposé triggered the decline. A federal jury found Holmes guilty on four counts of defrauding investors, and she was sentenced to 11 years and three months. Tomorrow's show covers AI and unemployment, and a family military legacy.
